1	# Embedded LLMs in Game Applications
2	
3	> Topic for `/teach`: how LLMs get plugged into games, what the engineering
4	> tradeoffs are, and how the choices map onto the code we just wrote.
5	
6	---
7	
8	## 1. The concept
9	
10	An **embedded LLM in a game** is a language model whose output is consumed by
11	the running game process — usually to generate NPC dialogue, narrate events,
12	or interpret freeform player input. "Embedded" in this context does **not**
13	necessarily mean the model lives inside the game's binary; it means the game
14	itself drives inference (vs. the user opening ChatGPT in another window).
15	There are three integration styles, and the choice shapes everything else:
16	
17	- **Cloud API call** (OpenAI, Anthropic, Inworld, Convai). The game POSTs JSON
18	  to a remote service. Easy to start, no install on the player's machine, best
19	  model quality. Costs money per token, requires internet, leaks user prompts
20	  to a third party, and adds 200-800 ms of latency per reply on top of
21	  generation time. Inworld and Convai are middleware that wrap this pattern
22	  specifically for game NPCs.
23	- **Sidecar process** (Ollama, LM Studio, llamafile, vLLM). A separate process
24	  on the player's machine hosts the model and exposes an HTTP API on
25	  `localhost`. The game stays small; model swaps are config changes. This is
26	  the easiest "fully local" path and what we picked for milestone 1.
27	- **In-process / embedded library** (`llama.cpp`, GGML, ONNX Runtime,
28	  candle-rs, MLC-LLM). The model lives inside the game binary, called directly
29	  through a C/C++ API. Lowest latency, no separate install for the player,
30	  full control over sampling and KV-cache management. Highest engineering
31	  cost: you own GPU detection, model loading, quantization formats, and
32	  thread management.
33	
34	Why this pattern at all? Pre-LLM NPCs used **dialogue trees** — finite,
35	hand-authored graphs of "if player picks option B, NPC says line 47." That
36	scales linearly with writer-hours and produces conversations that feel
37	canned after two playthroughs. LLM-driven NPCs trade authorial control for
38	combinatorial breadth: the same blacksmith can answer a question no writer
39	ever anticipated, in voice, because the persona prompt constrains *how* he
40	talks rather than *what* he can say. The tradeoff is loss of guarantees:
41	the NPC might hallucinate a quest item that doesn't exist, refuse to answer
42	in character, or — without guardrails — start discussing real-world topics.
43	**Persona prompting** plus **bounded history** is the cheap mitigation
44	(what we used); **structured output** (force JSON with allowed actions) and
45	**retrieval-augmented generation** (RAG, where the NPC's "memory" is a
46	searched knowledge base) are the heavier ones.
47	
48	Industry footprint as of 2026: AI Dungeon (2019, the original) ran on
49	GPT-2/3 cloud calls. *Suck Up!* (2023) shipped with cloud LLM-driven NPCs
50	behind a paywalled key. Modders shipped Skyrim and Stardew Valley LLM-NPC
51	mods using Ollama as a local sidecar. Roblox added cloud LLM "assistants"
52	into their creator tools. Nobody has shipped a AAA title with fully
53	embedded local LLMs yet, mostly because consumer GPU VRAM still limits how
54	big a model can ride along with a 6-8 GB game.
55	
56	---
57	
58	## 2. Minimal example
59	
60	The pattern below is the **whole** sidecar-LLM technique in 15 lines. It
61	posts a chat request to a local Ollama process and prints the reply. The
62	real game just wraps this in a worker thread and a reply queue.
63	
64	```cpp
65	#include "httplib.h"   // single-header HTTP client
66	#include "json.hpp"    // single-header JSON
67	using nlohmann::json;
68	
69	int main() {
70	    // 1. Build the chat body. "system" sets the persona; "user" is the player line.
71	    json body = {
72	        {"model", "qwen2.5:3b-instruct"},
73	        {"stream", false},
74	        {"messages", {
75	            {{"role", "system"}, {"content", "You are a gruff blacksmith. Reply in 1-2 sentences."}},
76	            {{"role", "user"},   {"content", "Have you seen any travelers today?"}},
77	        }},
78	    };
79	
80	    // 2. POST to Ollama's local HTTP API. No auth, no keys — it's on localhost.
81	    httplib::Client cli("localhost", 11434);
82	    auto res = cli.Post("/api/chat", body.dump(), "application/json");
83	
84	    // 3. Parse the reply. Ollama returns { "message": { "role", "content" }, ... }
85	    auto parsed = json::parse(res->body);
86	    std::cout << parsed["message"]["content"].get<std::string>() << "\n";
87	}
88	```
89	
90	What this example **does not** show but a real game needs:
91	- **Async**: the call above blocks for ~1-3 seconds. A game loop can't sit on
92	  it; you spin a worker thread and poll a reply queue.
93	- **History**: each NPC needs its own prior `messages[]` so context carries
94	  across turns. Without history every reply is amnesiac.
95	- **Bounding**: history grows forever if you let it. Cap to N recent turns
96	  or token-count-trim from the oldest.
97	- **Failure handling**: Ollama might not be running. The HTTP call might
98	  time out. The reply might be malformed JSON. None of that should crash
99	  the game.
100	
101	---
102	
103	## 3. How this maps onto our project
104	
105	Every bullet in the "real game needs" list above corresponds to a piece of
106	code we wrote. The teaching example is what `LlmClient::processOne()` would
107	look like with all the production concerns ripped out:
108	
109	| Concept                | Where it lives in our code |
110	| ---------------------- | -------------------------- |
111	| HTTP POST to Ollama    | `LlmClient.cpp` → `processOne()` |
112	| Persona as system prompt | `Persona.hpp` → `renderSystemPrompt()` |
113	| Per-NPC history        | `Npc.hpp` → `std::vector<ChatTurn> history_` |
114	| Bounded history (10 turns) | `Npc.cpp` → `trimHistory()` |
115	| Async via worker thread | `LlmClient.cpp` → `workerLoop()` |
116	| Game-loop-friendly polling | `LlmClient.cpp` → `drainReplies()` |
117	| Failure → in-character message | `main.cpp` → "[Wren seems distracted…]" |
118	
119	The structural decisions all trace back to one principle: **the LLM is an
120	external dependency that may be slow or absent, so it must be reachable
121	from any NPC through one chokepoint that owns its own thread.** That's
122	why `LlmClient` is a single object the whole game shares — not because
123	"singleton" is fashionable, but because Ollama can only sensibly serve
124	one request at a time on a single GPU, and centralizing the queue avoids
125	each NPC re-implementing the same thread-and-mutex dance.
126	
127	What we deliberately deferred — and why:
128	
129	- **Streaming**: Ollama supports `"stream": true`, which returns one JSON
130	  line per token. Lower perceived latency, more complex client. Add when
131	  the "thinking…" dwell time feels long.
132	- **Structured output**: we don't constrain the reply format. If we later
133	  want NPCs to emit `{"line": "...", "give_item": "rope"}`, switch to
134	  Ollama's `format: "json"` mode and validate against a schema.
135	- **In-process llama.cpp**: the public `LlmClient::submit / drainReplies`
136	  interface hides the transport. Swapping the body of `processOne()` from
137	  HTTP to a direct `llama_eval()` call is a one-file change.
138	
139	---
140	
141	## 4. The actual code (annotated against the concepts)
142	
143	Below is the heart of `LlmClient.cpp` with the concepts from §1-3 called
144	out inline. (The file in the repo has the same code with lighter
145	commentary.)
146	
147	```cpp
148	// Concept: SIDECAR INTEGRATION — game talks to Ollama via plain HTTP.
149	// Same shape as the minimal example, but wrapped in production concerns.
150	ChatReply LlmClient::processOne(const ChatRequest& req) {
151	    ChatReply reply;
152	    reply.id = req.id;
153	
154	    // Concept: PERSONA + HISTORY — every request is (system prompt) +
155	    // (prior turns) + (new user line). The persona makes the NPC stay in
156	    // character; the history makes the conversation feel continuous.
157	    json messages = json::array();
158	    if (!req.systemPrompt.empty()) {
159	        messages.push_back({{"role", "system"}, {"content", req.systemPrompt}});
160	    }
161	    for (const auto& turn : req.history) {
162	        messages.push_back({{"role", turn.role}, {"content", turn.content}});
163	    }
164	    messages.push_back({{"role", "user"}, {"content", req.userMessage}});
165	
166	    // stream=false → one big reply at the end. Switch to true for token-
167	    // by-token streaming later.
168	    json body = {
169	        {"model", config_.model},
170	        {"messages", messages},
171	        {"stream", false},
172	        {"options", {{"temperature", config_.temperature}}},
173	    };
174	
175	    // Concept: FAILURE-FRIENDLY TRANSPORT — bounded timeouts so a hung
176	    // Ollama can't freeze the worker thread.
177	    httplib::Client cli(config_.host, config_.port);
178	    cli.set_read_timeout(config_.requestTimeoutSeconds, 0);
179	    cli.set_connection_timeout(5, 0);
180	
181	    auto res = cli.Post("/api/chat", body.dump(), "application/json");
182	    if (!res) {                         // network failure
183	        reply.errorMessage = "could not reach Ollama";
184	        return reply;                   // ok stays false; UI handles it
185	    }
186	    // ... parse res->body into reply.content ...
187	    return reply;
188	}
189	```
190	
191	And the **async drain pattern** — the bit that lets a 60 fps game loop
192	talk to a model that takes seconds to reply:
193	
194	```cpp
195	// MAIN THREAD (game loop): submit the request, never wait for it.
196	companion.ask("Have you seen any travelers?");
197	ui.setThinking(true);
198	
199	// MAIN THREAD (next frame and every frame after): pull whatever has landed.
200	// Concept: ASYNC DRAIN — the worker thread populates a queue; the main
201	// thread empties it whenever convenient. No locks held across rendering.
202	for (const auto& reply : client.drainReplies()) {
203	    auto text = companion.onReplyArrived(reply);
204	    if (text) ui.appendLine({Kind::Npc, "Wren", *text});
205	    ui.setThinking(false);
206	}
207	```
208	
209	The worker thread (also in `LlmClient.cpp`) is the classic
210	condition-variable-driven queue consumer:
211	
212	```cpp
213	void LlmClient::workerLoop() {
214	    while (true) {
215	        ChatRequest req;
216	        {
217	            std::unique_lock<std::mutex> lock(requestMutex_);
218	            requestCv_.wait(lock, [this] { return stop_.load() || !requests_.empty(); });
219	            if (stop_.load() && requests_.empty()) return;
220	            req = std::move(requests_.front());
221	            requests_.pop();
222	        }
223	        ChatReply reply = processOne(req);   // the slow part: HTTP to Ollama
224	        {
225	            std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lock(replyMutex_);
226	            replies_.push_back(std::move(reply));
227	        }
228	    }
229	}
230	```
231	
232	Two separate mutexes (one for requests, one for replies) is intentional:
233	producer and consumer don't contend, and the main thread can drain replies
234	without ever blocking the worker mid-call.
235	
236	---
237	
238	## 5. Knowledge check
239	
240	Try answering these before peeking back at the doc. Good answers explain
241	the *why*, not just the *what*.
242	
243	1. **Why does each `Npc` keep its own conversation history rather than
244	   `LlmClient` keeping a single shared history?**
245	   *Hint: think about what happens when the player walks from Jim the
246	   pharmacist over to Jane the pedestrian and starts a new conversation.*
247	
248	2. **The minimal example in §2 would freeze the game loop for 1-3 seconds
249	   on every player line. What two pieces of machinery in our `LlmClient`
250	   prevent that, and what would happen if we removed either one?**
251	
252	3. **We picked Ollama as a sidecar instead of linking `llama.cpp` directly.
253	   Name one situation where that decision would be wrong, and one
254	   situation where it would still be right even after the game ships to
255	   players.**
256	
257	*(Sample answers are not included on purpose — write yours down and we can
258	talk through them.)*
259	
260	---
261	
262	## Further reading
263	
264	- [Ollama API reference](https://github.com/ollama/ollama/blob/main/docs/api.md) — the `/api/chat` endpoint we POST to.
265	- [`llama.cpp`](https://github.com/ggerganov/llama.cpp) — when you're ready to embed in-process.
266	- [`cpp-httplib`](https://github.com/yhirose/cpp-httplib) — the single-header HTTP client we vendored.
267	- [Inworld](https://inworld.ai) and [Convai](https://convai.com) — what the cloud-API approach looks like productized for games.
268	- [GBNF grammars](https://github.com/ggerganov/llama.cpp/blob/master/grammars/README.md) — how you'd enforce structured output (JSON, dialogue choices) when you graduate beyond freeform replies.
269

# Controls

All keys (except the mouse and a few fixed UI keys) can be rebound in-game:
press `Escape` → **Controls**, click a key chip, then press the new key.
Bindings are saved to `config/keybindings.cfg` immediately and can also be
edited there by hand.

## Defaults

| Action          | Default key | Config name     |
|-----------------|-------------|-----------------|
| Move forward    | `W`         | `move_forward`  |
| Move backward   | `S`         | `move_backward` |
| Strafe left     | `A`         | `strafe_left`   |
| Strafe right    | `D`         | `strafe_right`  |
| Talk to NPC     | `T`         | `talk`          |
| Open menu       | `Escape`    | `menu`          |

Mouse: look around (the cursor is captured while walking).

## Fixed keys

These always work regardless of bindings:

- `Escape` — leaves a conversation, backs out of menu pages, cancels a
  pending key capture. It is the universal "get me out" key.
- `Enter` — sends your typed line during a conversation.
- `Backspace` — deletes while typing.

## Conversations

1. Walk up to an NPC until `[T] Talk to <name>` appears.
2. Press the talk key. The world pauses input and a chat panel opens.
3. Type and press `Enter`. The NPC's reply streams in word by word.
4. Press `Escape` to walk away (mid-reply is fine — the NPC still finishes
   the thought and remembers it next time you talk).

## Rebinding rules

- Binding a key that another action already uses **swaps** the two keys; a
  toast in the menu tells you what swapped.
- Keys without a stable name (exotic media keys, etc.) are rejected.
- A broken or missing `config/keybindings.cfg` falls back to the defaults
  above; duplicate assignments in a hand-edited file are resolved in favor of
  the action listed first in the table.

1	# Developer Guide
2	
3	## Architecture: core / app split
4	
5	The codebase is split so that all game logic builds and tests on a headless
6	machine, while graphics stay isolated:
7	
8	```
9	src/core/   SFML-free, GL-free. Everything here is unit-tested.
10	src/app/    SFML + OpenGL. Only builds where graphics libs exist (Windows).
11	external/   Vendored single-header deps: httplib, nlohmann/json, doctest.
12	tests/      doctest suites + a plain-make runner for cmake-less containers.
13	personas/   One .persona file per NPC (identity + world placement).
14	config/     llm.cfg (model/host/latency) and keybindings.cfg.
15	```
16	
17	CMake builds the `llm_npc_core` static library unconditionally; the game
18	executable is added only when `SFML_FOUND AND OPENGL_FOUND`. Keep it that
19	way: **nothing in `src/core/` may include SFML or OpenGL headers.**
20	
21	### Core modules
22	
23	| Module            | Responsibility |
24	|-------------------|----------------|
25	| `LlmClient`       | One worker thread for all NPCs. Streams Ollama `/api/chat` (NDJSON); main thread polls `drainDeltas()` / `drainReplies()` per frame. `warmUp()` preloads the model; `keep_alive` keeps it resident. |
26	| `StreamAssembler` | Reassembles NDJSON lines from arbitrary TCP chunk boundaries; `parseOllamaChunk` maps one line to delta/done/error. |
27	| `Persona`         | Static NPC identity, rendered into the system prompt. |
28	| `PersonaLoader`   | Parses `personas/*.persona` (key=value header, `---`, free-form directives) including world placement. |
29	| `Npc`             | Per-NPC chat history (bounded), pending-request tracking, world placement. History only grows on successful replies. |

# Developer Guide

## Architecture: core / app split

The codebase is split so that all game logic builds and tests on a headless
machine, while graphics stay isolated:

```
src/core/   SFML-free, GL-free. Everything here is unit-tested.
src/app/    SFML + OpenGL. Only builds where graphics libs exist (Windows).
external/   Vendored single-header deps: httplib, nlohmann/json, doctest.
tests/      doctest suites + a plain-make runner for cmake-less containers.
personas/   One .persona file per NPC (identity + world placement).
config/     llm.cfg (model/host/latency) and keybindings.cfg.
```

CMake builds the `llm_npc_core` static library unconditionally; the game
executable is added only when `SFML_FOUND AND OPENGL_FOUND`. Keep it that
way: **nothing in `src/core/` may include SFML or OpenGL headers.**

### Core modules

| Module            | Responsibility |
|-------------------|----------------|
| `LlmClient`       | One worker thread for all NPCs. Streams Ollama `/api/chat` (NDJSON); main thread polls `drainDeltas()` / `drainReplies()` per frame. `warmUp()` preloads the model; `keep_alive` keeps it resident. |
| `StreamAssembler` | Reassembles NDJSON lines from arbitrary TCP chunk boundaries; `parseOllamaChunk` maps one line to delta/done/error. |
| `Persona`         | Static NPC identity, rendered into the system prompt. |
| `PersonaLoader`   | Parses `personas/*.persona` (key=value header, `---`, free-form directives) including world placement. |
| `Npc`             | Per-NPC chat history (bounded), pending-request tracking, world placement. History only grows on successful replies. |
| `City`            | Building AABBs + circle collision with axis-separated slide (`resolveMovement`). |
| `World`           | City + NPC roster; `nearestNpcWithin` drives the talk prompt. |
| `DialogueSession` | Roaming → Talking → WaitingReply → Streaming state machine; routes streamed deltas by request id. |
| `KeyBindings`     | Action → key-name map with swap-on-conflict rebinding and file persistence. Names are translated to SFML codes only in `src/app/InputMap`. |
| `Config`          | Tiny key=value reader + `llm.cfg` loader. |

### App modules

- `Renderer3D` — legacy GL 2.1 immediate mode, procedural textures, the
  first-person camera, and `worldToScreen` for SFML nameplates.
- `main.cpp` — mode machine (Playing / Dialogue / Menu) and the frame loop:
  GL 3D pass → `pushGLStates()` → SFML overlay → `popGLStates()` → `display()`.
  Always restore that order; mixing raw GL with SFML drawing outside the
  push/pop pair corrupts state.
- `DialogUI` — chat overlay with live streaming line; `swallowNextTextEntered()`
  keeps the talk key's character out of the input box.
- `Menu` — mouse-driven pause menu and key rebinding.
- `InputMap` — portable key-name ↔ `sf::Keyboard::Key` table.

## Building and testing

### Container / Linux (no SFML needed)

```sh
make -C tests test          # builds core + all unit tests with g++, runs them
```

The make runner is the primary gate: run it before every commit. It compiles
`src/core/*.cpp` + `tests/test_*.cpp` with `-Wall -Wextra -pthread`.

Tests run fully offline: `tests/FakeOllama.hpp` spins an in-process
`httplib::Server` on a random port that speaks the Ollama streaming protocol,
including error modes and chunk boundaries that split JSON lines mid-token.

Live end-to-end tests (real Ollama on localhost) are opt-in:

```sh
OLLAMA_LIVE=1 make -C tests test            # uses qwen2.5:3b-instruct
OLLAMA_TEST_MODEL=llama3.2:1b OLLAMA_LIVE=1 make -C tests test
```

### Windows (full game)

```bat
run.bat        # double-clickable: checks MSYS2 + Ollama, cmake, build, play
```

or the equivalent `run.ps1`. Requires MSYS2 UCRT64 with `mingw-w64-ucrt-x86_64-{gcc,cmake,sfml}` and an Ollama install with the model pulled.

```sh
cmake -S . -B build -G "MinGW Makefiles" && cmake --build build -j
ctest --test-dir build        # same doctest suites via cmake
```

## Latency playbook

Findings applied from the sibling games and the original companion demo:

1. **Stream replies** (`"stream": true`): first words render ~10x sooner than
   waiting for the full completion.
2. **`keep_alive=10m`** (config/llm.cfg): the model stays in RAM between
   conversations; without it every chat pays a multi-second reload.
3. **`warmUp()` at boot**: an empty-messages request forces the load while
   the player is still walking around.
4. **One worker thread, non-blocking drains**: the render loop never waits on
   the network; 60 FPS is independent of Ollama health.
5. Small default model (`qwen2.5:3b-instruct`) — swap via `config/llm.cfg`.

## Adding an NPC

1. Create `personas/<id>.persona` (see existing files; `name` is required,
   `position`/`facing`/`spot` place them in the world).
2. Pick a free spot — `tests/test_world.cpp` has a placement-sanity pattern;
   NPCs must not stand inside a building AABB.
3. That's it: the roster is whatever `personas/` contains, sorted by filename.
   Palette color comes from roster order (`Renderer3D::kNpcPalettes`).

## Conventions

- Commits: `type(scope): description`, small (2-3 files), pushed to the
  feature branch — never to main.
- Every public function carries a doc comment; no TODOs in committed code.
- New core logic requires doctest coverage in the same or the following
  commit.

Lesson 0001 · LLM NPC City

How to Run and Develop

Why this matters: every change you make to the game must be built, tested, and verified. Two environments exist — knowing when to use each saves hours of confusion.

Progress: 0 / 6 sections complete 0%
1

The two environments

This project runs in two completely separate environments and you use them for different jobs. Mixing them up is the #1 source of "why doesn't this work?" moments.

┌─────────────────────────────┐ ┌─────────────────────────────┐ │ Linux / Dev Container │ │ Windows (your machine) │ │ │ │ │ │ g++, make, git, curl │ │ MSYS2 UCRT64 + SFML │ │ NO cmake, NO SFML │ │ Ollama (model loaded) │ │ │ │ │ │ → make -C tests test │ │ → run.bat (double-click) │ │ (fast, offline) │ │ (builds + plays) │ └─────────────────────────────┘ └─────────────────────────────┘ primary dev loop visual + play verification

Container / Linux is where you write code and run the unit tests. All 57 tests run in under two seconds, fully offline — no Ollama, no SFML, no window. This is your main feedback loop.

Windows is where the game actually renders. The 3D city, the NPC figures, the dialogue overlay — none of that can be verified without SFML and OpenGL. You push your commits, then pull and run run.bat on Windows to see how it looks.

Key rule
Logic in src/core/ is tested in the container. Visual behaviour in src/app/ is verified on Windows. Never reverse this.
2

Running the game on Windows

All prerequisites must be in place first. Here is the full one-time setup and the daily run flow.

One-time setup

  1. Install Ollama from https://ollama.com/download, then in any terminal:
    ollama pull qwen2.5:3b-instruct
    This pulls a ~2 GB model. It only happens once (or when you want to try a different model).
  2. Install MSYS2 from https://www.msys2.org. Open the UCRT64 shell (not the default MSYS shell — ucrt64 specifically) and run: 
    pacman -S mingw-w64-ucrt-x86_64-gcc \
           mingw-w64-ucrt-x86_64-cmake \
           mingw-w64-ucrt-x86_64-sfml
    This gives you the compiler, build system, and graphics library the game needs.
  3. Clone the repo (if you haven't): 
    git clone https://github.com/bjl14710/cpp_game_with_llm_npcs.git
cd cpp_game_with_llm_npcs
git checkout initial_npcs_and_world

Every time you want to play

  1. Make sure Ollama is running: ollama serve in a terminal (or it may already be running as a service).
  2. Double-click run.bat in the repo folder. That's it.

What run.bat actually does, step by step:

REM 1. Sets MSYS2 ucrt64 tools on PATH so cmake and g++ can be found
set "PATH=C:\msys64\ucrt64\bin;%PATH%"

REM 2. Checks Ollama is reachable — if not, prints a helpful error and pauses
curl -fsS --max-time 2 "http://localhost:11434/api/tags"

REM 3. Configures the build (only matters the first time or after CMakeLists changes)
cmake -S . -B build -G "MinGW Makefiles"

REM 4. Compiles everything (parallel, fast on second run since CMake is incremental)
cmake --build build -j

REM 5. Runs the game
build\cpp_game_with_llm_npcs.exe
Common issue
If you get "MSYS2 ucrt64 toolchain not found", the MSYS2 install is at a non-default path or you installed the wrong variant. run.bat looks for C:\msys64\ucrt64\bin — check that path exists.
3

The development loop (day-to-day)

You will spend most of your time in the container (Linux), not on Windows. Here is the cycle:

  1. Edit code in src/core/ or tests/
  2. Run tests — one command, takes ~1 second: 
    make -C tests test
    You'll see each compiled file scroll by, then a pass/fail summary from doctest.
  3. Fix any failures, then repeat steps 1–2 until green.
  4. Commit and push — small commits (2–3 files): 
    git add src/core/Npc.hpp src/core/Npc.cpp
git commit -m "feat(core): add patrol state to Npc"
git push origin initial_npcs_and_world
  5. On Windows: git pull, then run.bat to see it rendered.

What the test command actually runs

The command make -C tests test is shorthand for "run the Makefile inside the tests/ directory, targeting the test rule." That Makefile does:

  1. Compiles every src/core/*.cpp file
  2. Compiles every tests/test_*.cpp file
  3. Links them all into tests/build/run_tests
  4. Executes that binary — doctest reports results

Notice it does not compile anything in src/app/. That is intentional — the app layer needs SFML which is not in the container.

Current state
57 tests, 402 assertions — all pass in this repo as of lesson creation. If you add new logic to src/core/, add tests in the same commit.
4

The core / app split — why it's designed this way

The repo's source tree is divided into two halves with a hard rule between them:

FolderContainsAllowed to useTested by
src/core/All game logicstdlib, httplib, json, pthreadsdoctest in container
src/app/Graphics + inputSFML, OpenGL, plus coreManual on Windows

The rule: nothing in src/core/ may include an SFML or OpenGL header. Ever.

Why does this matter? Because SFML cannot be installed in the container. If City.cpp included <SFML/Graphics.hpp>, the test suite would fail to compile and you'd have no automated safety net. The split buys you:

  • Fast offline tests — all logic is reachable from the container, no GUI needed.
  • Portability — the core could be ported to a mobile game, a web server, a CLI tool. The app layer is the only part that is Windows-locked.
  • Confidence before you see it — when NPC collision or dialogue logic is green in tests, you know it's correct before you ever run the game.

The CMake structure mirrors this split

# llm_npc_core: always builds, no SFML
add_library(llm_npc_core STATIC
    src/core/City.cpp    src/core/Config.cpp
    src/core/LlmClient.cpp  src/core/Npc.cpp  # ... etc
)

# Game executable: only built where SFML + OpenGL exist
if(SFML_FOUND AND OPENGL_FOUND)
    add_executable(cpp_game_with_llm_npcs
        src/app/main.cpp  src/app/Renderer3D.cpp  # ...
    )
    target_link_libraries(...  llm_npc_core  sfml-graphics ...)
endif()

How to Run and Develop

Why this matters: every change you make to the game must be built, tested, and verified. Two environments exist — knowing when to use each saves hours of confusion.

1

The two environments

This project runs in two completely separate environments and you use them for different jobs. Mixing them up is the #1 source of "why doesn't this work?" moments.

┌─────────────────────────────┐ ┌─────────────────────────────┐ │ Linux / Dev Container │ │ Windows (your machine) │ │ │ │ │ │ g++, make, git, curl │ │ MSYS2 UCRT64 + SFML │ │ NO cmake, NO SFML │ │ Ollama (model loaded) │ │ │ │ │ │ → make -C tests test │ │ → run.bat (double-click) │ │ (fast, offline) │ │ (builds + plays) │ └─────────────────────────────┘ └─────────────────────────────┘ primary dev loop visual + play verification

Container / Linux is where you write code and run the unit tests. All 57 tests run in under two seconds, fully offline — no Ollama, no SFML, no window. This is your main feedback loop.

Windows is where the game actually renders. The 3D city, the NPC figures, the dialogue overlay — none of that can be verified without SFML and OpenGL. You push your commits, then pull and run run.bat on Windows to see how it looks.

Key rule
Logic in src/core/ is tested in the container. Visual behaviour in src/app/ is verified on Windows. Never reverse this.
2

Running the game on Windows

All prerequisites must be in place first. Here is the full one-time setup and the daily run flow.

One-time setup

  1. Install Ollama from https://ollama.com/download, then in any terminal:
    ollama pull qwen2.5:3b-instruct
    This pulls a ~2 GB model. It only happens once (or when you want to try a different model).
  2. Install MSYS2 from https://www.msys2.org. Open the UCRT64 shell (not the default MSYS shell — ucrt64 specifically) and run: 
    pacman -S mingw-w64-ucrt-x86_64-gcc \
           mingw-w64-ucrt-x86_64-cmake \
           mingw-w64-ucrt-x86_64-sfml
    This gives you the compiler, build system, and graphics library the game needs.
  3. Clone the repo (if you haven't): 
    git clone https://github.com/bjl14710/cpp_game_with_llm_npcs.git
cd cpp_game_with_llm_npcs
git checkout initial_npcs_and_world

Every time you want to play

  1. Make sure Ollama is running: ollama serve in a terminal (or it may already be running as a service).
  2. Double-click run.bat in the repo folder. That's it.

What run.bat actually does, step by step:

REM 1. Sets MSYS2 ucrt64 tools on PATH so cmake and g++ can be found
set "PATH=C:\msys64\ucrt64\bin;%PATH%"

REM 2. Checks Ollama is reachable — if not, prints a helpful error and pauses
curl -fsS --max-time 2 "http://localhost:11434/api/tags"

REM 3. Configures the build (only matters the first time or after CMakeLists changes)
cmake -S . -B build -G "MinGW Makefiles"

REM 4. Compiles everything (parallel, fast on second run since CMake is incremental)
cmake --build build -j

REM 5. Runs the game
build\cpp_game_with_llm_npcs.exe
Common issue
If you get "MSYS2 ucrt64 toolchain not found", the MSYS2 install is at a non-default path or you installed the wrong variant. run.bat looks for C:\msys64\ucrt64\bin — check that path exists.
3

The development loop (day-to-day)

You will spend most of your time in the container (Linux), not on Windows. Here is the cycle:

  1. Edit code in src/core/ or tests/
  2. Run tests — one command, takes ~1 second: 
    make -C tests test
    You'll see each compiled file scroll by, then a pass/fail summary from doctest.
  3. Fix any failures, then repeat steps 1–2 until green.
  4. Commit and push — small commits (2–3 files): 
    git add src/core/Npc.hpp src/core/Npc.cpp
git commit -m "feat(core): add patrol state to Npc"
git push origin initial_npcs_and_world
  5. On Windows: git pull, then run.bat to see it rendered.

What the test command actually runs

The command make -C tests test is shorthand for "run the Makefile inside the tests/ directory, targeting the test rule." That Makefile does:

  1. Compiles every src/core/*.cpp file
  2. Compiles every tests/test_*.cpp file
  3. Links them all into tests/build/run_tests
  4. Executes that binary — doctest reports results

Notice it does not compile anything in src/app/. That is intentional — the app layer needs SFML which is not in the container.

Current state
57 tests, 402 assertions — all pass in this repo as of lesson creation. If you add new logic to src/core/, add tests in the same commit.

The repo's source tree is divided into two halves with a hard rule between them:

FolderContainsAllowed to useTested by
src/core/All game logicstdlib, httplib, json, pthreadsdoctest in container
src/app/Graphics + inputSFML, OpenGL, plus coreManual on Windows

  • Fast offline tests — all logic is reachable from the container, no GUI needed.
  • Portability — the core could be ported to a mobile game, a web server, a CLI tool. The app layer is the only part that is Windows-locked.
  • Confidence before you see it — when NPC collision or dialogue logic is green in tests, you know it's correct before you ever run the game.

content.text:
No brew needed anywhere in this project — everything on Windows goes through MSYS2 UCRT64. The only package manager you need is `pacman` inside the MSYS2 UCRT64 shell:

```
pacman -S mingw-w64-ucrt-x86_64-gcc mingw-w64-ucrt-x86_64-cmake mingw-w64-ucrt-x86_64-sfml
```

Then `run.bat` handles the rest. No Homebrew, no vcpkg, nothing else.
